content: In chemistry, isomers are compounds that share the same molecular formula but differ in their structural arrangements. These structural differences can lead to variations in their physical and chemical properties, especially if the functional groups are not identical. It is important to distinguish chemical isomers from nuclear isomers, which involve atomic nuclei in different energy states. Isomers can be classified into various types, such as stereoisomers, enantiomers, and geometrical isomers. For example, propanol (C3H8O) exists as two isomers: propan-1-ol (n-propyl alcohol) and propan-2-ol (isopropyl alcohol). The difference lies in the position of the oxygen atom, which is attached to an end carbon in propan-1-ol and to the central carbon in propan-2-ol. Another isomer of C3H8O, methoxyethane (methyl-ethyl-ether), has significantly different properties because its oxygen atom is bonded to two carbons instead of one carbon and one hydrogen, making it an ether rather than an alcohol. Some isomers exhibit more subtle differences in properties. For instance, theobromine, found in chocolate, is a vasodilator with effects similar to caffeine. However, moving one of its methyl groups to a different position on its molecular structure results in the isomer theophylline, which has distinct pharmacological effects, including bronchodilation and anti-inflammatory properties. Isomers can also differ in the types of chemical bonds they contain. For example, allene contains two double bonds, while propyne contains one triple bond. Isomerism is broadly categorized into structural isomerism and stereoisomerism. Structural isomers differ in the connectivity of their atoms and functional groups. Examples include chain isomerism (variations in hydrocarbon chain branching), position isomerism (differences in the position of functional groups), and functional group isomerism (different functional groups derived from the same molecular formula). Stereoisomers, on the other hand, have the same bond structure but differ in the spatial arrangement of atoms. This category includes enantiomers, which are non-superimposable mirror images, and diastereomers, which are not mirror images. Diastereomers can be further divided into conformational isomers (interconvertible by bond rotations) and cis-trans isomers (not interconvertible by simple bond rotations). Skeletal isomerism involves differences in the main carbon chain structure, often seen in secondary and tertiary alcohols. Tautomers are a special type of structural isomers that spontaneously interconvert, such as keto-enol tautomers, where a proton shifts between a carbon and an oxygen atom. Tautomers exhibit distinct chemical properties and reactions, but if the interconversion is rapid, they cannot be isolated. In medicinal chemistry and biochemistry, cis-trans isomerism and enantiomerism are particularly significant. Enantiomers are of great interest because they often exhibit different biological activities. For example, enzymes can distinguish between enantiomers, and living organisms frequently prefer one enantiomer over the other. Enantiomers may also differ in their ability to rotate polarized light. Chromatographic methods have been developed to separate enantiomers, but these techniques are costly and are primarily used to remove harmful or biologically inactive enantiomers. Other types of isomerism include topological isomerism, where large molecules form different shapes, such as knots or loops, as seen in catenanes and DNA. Topoisomerase enzymes can alter DNA topology by creating or removing knots. Isotopomers, or isotopic isomers, differ in the positions of isotopic substitutions within the molecule. In nuclear physics, nuclear isomers refer to excited states of atomic nuclei. The concept of isomerism was first observed in 1827 when Friedrich Wöhler prepared cyanic acid and noted its identical elemental composition to fulminic acid, despite their differing properties. This discovery challenged the prevailing belief that compounds with the same elemental composition must be identical. Jöns Jakob Berzelius later introduced the term isomerism to describe this phenomenon. In 1849, Louis Pasteur separated tartaric acid crystals into two mirror-image forms, which were later identified as optical stereoisomers that rotate polarized light in opposite directions.
